prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The search will continue until at least Friday night for 16 people missing since Thursday morning when a helicopter carrying them to an offshore oil platform ditched in the Atlantic Ocean off Newfoundland, Canadian officials said. A helicopter made an emergency crash landing off Newfoundland en route to Hibernia oil field on Thursday. One survivor, identified as Robert Decker, was found and taken to a hospital, but efforts to find more survivors had proven fruitless, said Maj. Denis McGuire of the Rescue Coordination Center in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The body of one person, who has not been identified publicly, also was pulled from the water. There were 18 people aboard the helicopter when it went down, about 30 nautical miles from St. John's. "All we've got is the debris field," McGuire said. "There are no indications of any [more] survivors, but the search will continue." The water is 400 feet deep at the site where the helicopter hit the water, he said. Helicopters and ships were scouring the debris field Thursday evening, and search-and-rescue technicians were planning to use night-vision goggles and flares overnight. The debris filled a six-mile area, said Jeri Grychowski of the Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax. Officials became aware that the helicopter was having problems shortly after 9:10 a.m., when the pilot declared a mayday, McGuire said. "They declared their mayday and then they hit the water or landed in the water approximately eight minutes later," he said. About 25 minutes later, a helicopter arrived and discovered the survivor, the body, the overturned helicopter and two empty life rafts, he said. Those aboard should have have been wearing survival suits that would have kept them dry and were equipped with lights and personal locator beacons, but the suits have not helped searchers. "We have not received any signals whatsoever," McGuire said. The suits theoretically would allow wearers to survive 24 hours in the freezing waters -- or until about 9 a.m. Friday -- but the search effort was to continue well beyond that. "We will continue to search until there's absolutely no chance that any survivors will be located," he said. "Until last light [Friday]." At that time, based on water temperature and the size of the search area, officials will decide whether to continue the effort, he said. Early in the day, high winds and seas hampered the search, but by late afternoon, the weather had improved, though seas were still about 13 to 16 feet (4 to 5 meters) and winds were at about 40 knots (46 mph). The survivor was taken to the Health Sciences Center in St. John's, Newfoundland. The helicopter had been heading to the Hibernia offshore oil platform when it went down in what Grychowski called a controlled emergency crash landing. The pilot reported some technical malfunctions before the crash and radioed that he was turning the chopper around, said Rick Burt of Cougar Helicopters -- the operator of the S-92 Sikorsky copter.

The aircraft had been transporting them to the offshore Hibernia oil platform when it made a controlled emergency landing on the water.

Of the 18 people aboard, one survivor—Robert Decker—was rescued and transported to a hospital. The body of another person, whose identity had not been publicly released, was also recovered. Maj. Denis McGuire of the Rescue Coordination Center in Halifax, Nova Scotia, said no additional survivors had been found.

The helicopter came down roughly 30 nautical miles from St. John’s, in an area where the ocean is about 400 feet deep. McGuire said rescuers had located only a field of wreckage and had seen no evidence of further survivors, although the operation would continue.

McGuire said the helicopter entered or landed on the water about eight minutes later. Approximately 25 minutes after that, another helicopter reached the scene and found Decker, the recovered body, the overturned aircraft and two unoccupied life rafts.

Those on board were expected to have been wearing survival suits designed to keep them dry. The suits also contained lights and personal locator beacons, but rescuers had received no signals from them, McGuire said.

In theory, the suits could keep someone alive for 24 hours in the frigid ocean—until around 9 a.m. Friday—but authorities intended to search well past that point. McGuire said the effort would continue until there was no remaining possibility of finding survivors, at least until the final daylight Friday. Officials would then assess whether to carry on, taking into account the water temperature and the extent of the search zone.

Strong winds and rough seas impeded operations earlier Thursday. Conditions improved by late afternoon, although waves were still approximately 13 to 16 feet (4 to 5 meters) high and winds were near 40 knots, or 46 mph.

Decker was brought to the Health Sciences Center in St. John’s, Newfoundland.

Grychowski characterized the incident as a controlled emergency landing. Before the helicopter went down, the pilot reported technical problems and said the aircraft was turning back, according to Rick Burt of Cougar Helicopters, which operated the S-92 Sikorsky helicopter.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS: Helicopter crashes off Newfoundland; 16 missing**

**ST. JOHN’S, Newfoundland** — Search-and-rescue crews are combing the frigid North Atlantic after a helicopter carrying 18 people crashed off the coast of Newfoundland, authorities said.

One survivor has been rescued and transported to a hospital in critical condition. Crews have also recovered one body, while 16 people remain missing.

The Sikorsky S-92 helicopter was transporting offshore oil workers when it went down southeast of St. John’s. Officials said the aircraft had reported mechanical trouble before contact was lost.

Military aircraft, Coast Guard vessels and other emergency crews are searching the crash area. Debris and life rafts have been spotted in the water, but harsh conditions and extremely cold temperatures are complicating rescue efforts.

Authorities have not yet released the names of everyone aboard. The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

This is a developing story.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the search-and-rescue response after a Cougar Helicopters S-92 ditched in the Atlantic while traveling to the Hibernia offshore oil platform.
counterfactuals.output:
On March 12, 2009, Cougar Helicopters Flight 91 declared an emergency after losing main-gearbox oil pressure while en route from St. John’s to the Hibernia platform. The S-92 turned back but ditched about 55 kilometres southeast of St. John’s and sank rapidly.

The Joint Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax coordinated the response. Cougar aircraft, Canadian Armed Forces Cormorant helicopters and Hercules aircraft, Canadian Coast Guard vessels, offshore supply ships, and other nearby aircraft and vessels were sent to the area. A Cougar helicopter was among the first aircraft to locate the wreckage and people in the water; a military Cormorant subsequently recovered the sole survivor, Robert Decker, who had spent roughly an hour in the near-freezing Atlantic.

Searchers recovered the bodies of the other 17 occupants and continued searching for debris and evidence. The operation was hindered by cold water, wind, waves, the aircraft’s rapid sinking, and the failure of most occupants to escape or reach a life raft. The tragedy prompted scrutiny of offshore rescue readiness, including response times and the lack at that time of a dedicated, immediately available offshore search-and-rescue helicopter near St. John’s.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining what happened when a helicopter carrying 18 people made an emergency landing about 30 nautical miles from St. John’s, Newfoundland.
counterfactuals.output:
# Helicopter carrying 18 lands safely in St. John’s after in-flight emergency

**ST. JOHN’S, N.L.** — A helicopter carrying 18 people made a safe emergency landing at St. John’s International Airport after encountering a problem roughly 30 nautical miles—about 56 kilometres—from the Newfoundland capital.

The aircraft was carrying 16 passengers and two crew members on an offshore flight when the pilots received an indication of a possible mechanical or technical problem. The crew declared an emergency, turned the helicopter back toward St. John’s and followed established emergency procedures.

Emergency personnel were positioned at the airport before the helicopter arrived. Despite the heightened response, the aircraft landed without further incident, and everyone on board got out safely. No injuries were reported.

The helicopter was taken out of service so maintenance personnel could inspect it and determine what triggered the cockpit warning. The initial emergency declaration did not necessarily mean that a critical system had failed; aviation crews are trained to declare emergencies early when warning systems indicate a potential problem, particularly during flights over the North Atlantic.

Helicopters serving Newfoundland and Labrador’s offshore petroleum industry routinely carry workers between St. John’s and installations hundreds of kilometres at sea. The flights operate under strict safety rules because much of the route is over cold, open water and can be affected by rapidly changing weather.

Passengers on such flights wear survival suits, and aircraft carry emergency equipment designed for offshore operations. Operators also have procedures for turning back, diverting or ditching if a problem cannot be resolved in the air.

The safe landing meant no search-and-rescue operation was required. Aviation authorities were expected to review the occurrence, while the operator’s maintenance and safety teams examined the aircraft before any return to service.

The incident ended without injuries, but it prompted a full airport emergency response because of the number of people aboard and the risks associated with an offshore helicopter reporting a possible technical malfunction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the Newfoundland offshore helicopter accident, including the mayday timeline, weather conditions, survival suits, debris field, casualties, and how long officials plan to continue searching.
counterfactuals.output:
### Newfoundland offshore helicopter accident

On March 12, 2009, Cougar Helicopters Flight 491, a Sikorsky S‑92A carrying offshore oil workers from St. John’s, crashed in the Atlantic about 55–65 kilometres southeast of Newfoundland.

- **Mayday timeline:** At about **9:40 a.m. Newfoundland time**, the crew declared a mayday after reporting **zero oil pressure in the main gearbox** and began returning to St. John’s. Roughly five minutes later, the pilots said they were **ditching**. Contact was then lost, and the helicopter went down shortly before **9:50 a.m.**
- **Weather and sea conditions:** Visibility was reported as relatively good, but winds were around **35–40 km/h**, seas were approximately **two to three metres**, and the water temperature was near freezing.
- **Survival suits:** All **18 people aboard**—16 passengers and two pilots—were believed to be wearing cold-water immersion suits. The suits increased survival time but did not eliminate the danger from near-freezing water, injuries, or suit leakage.
- **Debris field:** Search crews found a substantial debris field containing pieces of the aircraft and flotation equipment, including life rafts, but initially saw no intact fuselage.
- **Casualties:** One passenger, **Robert Decker**, was rescued alive. One body was recovered during the initial search; the other 16 occupants were initially listed as missing. The final toll was **17 dead and one survivor**.
- **Length of search:** Search-and-rescue officials said they would continue the intensive search for **at least 24 hours**, through the night and into the following day, before reassessing whether it should remain a rescue operation.

counterfactuals.output:
**Search continues for 17 missing after helicopter crashes off Newfoundland**

ST. JOHN’S, Newfoundland — Canadian rescue crews searched the North Atlantic for 17 people missing after a Sikorsky helicopter carrying offshore oil workers crashed Thursday while flying from St. John’s to installations including the Hibernia oil field, officials said.

The Cougar Helicopters aircraft was carrying 16 passengers and two crew members when it went down about 55 kilometers (34 miles) southeast of St. John’s, according to the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax.

One person was pulled from the water and taken to a hospital, officials said. There was no immediate word on the condition of the survivor.

Military aircraft, coast guard vessels and civilian ships were sent to the area to search for the others. Rescue officials said crews had found debris and empty life rafts.

The helicopter reported a problem with oil pressure in its main gearbox and was attempting to return to St. John’s when contact was lost, transportation officials said. The Sikorsky S-92A had been bound for the SeaRose production vessel and the Hibernia platform.

Officials said the search was continuing despite cold water and difficult conditions. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said it was sending investigators to determine the cause of the crash.

Cougar Helicopters said it was cooperating with authorities and had begun notifying the passengers’ families. Offshore flights were suspended following the accident.
